Under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), the difference between being Authorized and Notified by the Malta Financial Services Authority (MFSA) dictates how a firm can provide cross-border Reception and Transmission of Orders (RTO) for crypto-assets on behalf of clients:

Authorized (CASP): Standalone crypto firms must obtain a full Crypto-Asset Service Provider (CASP) License. To offer RTO cross-border in the EU/EEA, authorized CASPs must formally notify the MFSA of their target host states. The MFSA then passports the service.

Notified (Exempt Entities): Traditional financial institutions (e.g., credit institutions, investment firms, MiFID II entities) do not need a new, separate CASP license. Instead, they rely on their existing licenses and are only required to notify the MFSA at least 40 days prior to offering cross-border crypto RTO

Your traditional financial institution license suffices.Passporting Process: Your RTO service is not "passported" in the traditional sense; instead, you rely on a prior notification to the MFSA instead of seeking a new approval for host states.Time-to-Market: Instead of waiting for the full CASP licensing and formal passporting clearance, you only need to submit an advance notice 40 days before commencing cross-border RTO services in target EU/EEA host states.Ongoing Supervision: You remain supervised primarily under your original regulatory framework (e.g., MiFID II) rather than being subject to standalone CASP compliance rulebooks, while ensuring adherence to MiCA's conduct-of-business rules for crypto.

That's how it was discovered, the various armies in WW1 were giving their millions of conscripts batteries of aptitude tests to quickly slot them into the various specialties that technology was creating. But they discovered that the people who were good at one skill tended to be good at all of them, and vice versa for those that were bad at one skill tended to be bad at all of them. They calculated this baseline score that crossed multiple independent tests and called it General Intelligence, which is what IQ tests attempt to measure - the generalizable effect of an individual's intelligence.
